# Intercurrent Events {#sec-Intercurrent_Events}
Intercurrent events are events that occur after treatment initiation and either prevent the endpoint from being observed or change its interpretation. Common examples include treatment discontinuation, use of rescue medication, switching to another therapy, and death. Because these events affect what the endpoint actually measures, they must be identified in advance and each one paired with a treatment strategy (see @sec-Treatment_Strategies) that describes how it is handled in the estimand. Ignoring intercurrent events, or handling them implicitly, leaves the treatment effect ambiguous. Depending on the treatment strategy, the treatment effect may be interpreted as the effect of treatment in the presence of the intercurrent event, or as the effect that would have been seen had the event not occurred. The estimand framework makes these choices explicit, and it is important to ensure that the chosen strategy matches the clinical question of interest.


## Adverse Events {#sec-Adverse_Events}
An adverse event (AE) is any unfavourable medical occurrence in a subject during the trial, whether or not it is considered related to the treatment [@ICHE2A]. AEs become intercurrent events when they lead to actions that affect the endpoint (see @sec-Endpoints), such as dose reduction, treatment discontinuation, or initiation of rescue medication. The chosen treatment strategy (see @sec-Treatment_Strategies) determines how these situations enter the analysis: a treatment policy strategy keeps the observed outcome regardless of the event, whereas a hypothetical strategy targets the outcome that would have been seen had the event not occurred. Distinguishing the AE itself from the clinical response to it is essential for defining a coherent estimand.

### Serious Adverse Events {#sec-Serious_Adverse_Events}
A serious adverse event (SAE) is one that meets at least one regulatory seriousness criterion: it results in death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalisation, causes persistent or significant disability, leads to a congenital anomaly, or is otherwise judged medically important [@ICHE2A]. Seriousness reflects the outcome or severity of consequences, not the causal relationship to treatment. SAEs often drive intercurrent events such as treatment discontinuation or death, and they carry expedited reporting obligations, so their handling in the estimand and their pathway through safety surveillance must both be considered.

### Adverse Events of Special Interest {#sec-Adverse_Events_of_Special_Interest}
An AE of special interest is a pre-specified event, whether serious or not, that warrants closer monitoring because of a known or suspected association with the treatment. These events are defined in advance in the trial protocol (see @sec-Clinical_Trial_Protocol), often through standardised medical queries, and may trigger additional data collection or independent review. Identifying them prospectively allows consistent capture across the programme and supports focused benefit-risk assessment.
